summary: This Wikipedia-derived note surveys imperialism across history and regions, covering its theoretical framing (Gallagher and Robinson's 'informal empire' concept, environmental determinism as justification), and the imperial histories of Germany, Russia/Soviet Union, the Ottoman Empire, Japan, France and Britain. It also notes earlier and non-European empires such as those of Genghis Khan, the Aztecs and Incas, and African empires. The note ends with the British East India Company and the rise and decline of the First and later British Empires.
one_line: Overview of imperialism as a concept and historical phenomenon, spanning European, Soviet, Ottoman, Japanese, and other empires from antiquity to the 20th century.
key_facts: Historians John Gallagher (1919–1980) and Ronald Robinson (1920–1999) constructed a framework for understanding European imperialism during the 20th century.
Gallagher and Robinson's key idea was empire 'informally if possible and formally if necessary.'
Environmental determinism served as a moral justification for domination, with people in tropical environments seen as 'less civilized', justifying colonial control as a civilizing mission.
Otto von Bismarck (1862–90) long opposed colonial acquisitions, arguing colonies did not pay for themselves and would distract Germany from Europe.
Lenin famously declared that Imperialism was the highest stage of capitalism.
Joseph Stalin established 'socialism in one country' for the Soviet Union after Lenin's death.
In a speech at the UN conference in 1960, Nikita Khrushchev announced the continuation of the war on imperialism.

The Ottoman Empire lasted from 1299 to 1923 and at the height of its power under Suleiman the Magnificent controlled much of Southeast Europe, Western Asia, the Caucasus, North Africa, and the Horn of Africa.
The British East India Company was established in 1599 and chartered by Queen Elizabeth in the following year.
During the First Sino-Japanese War in 1894, Japan absorbed Taiwan.
Korea was annexed by Japan in 1910.
In 1931 Japan conquered Manchuria from China.
Charles de Gaulle decided to grant Algeria independence in 1962 even though France had won the war in Algeria.
Nearly all of France's colonies gained independence by 1960, but France retained great financial and diplomatic influence.
The First British Empire's growth was reversed by the loss of the American colonies in 1776.
By the 1840s, Britain had adopted a highly successful policy of free trade.
